utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if I can, I'll try to quickly go through some of the principal discrepancies and try to keep the record clear as to page numbers. I'm not sure... It might be possible that he was introduced to me as uncle, "Daja," if I remember it well." [sic] "... but for the period we met," a little further on, "it's not clear whether he was introduced to me as Daja because it was short. It was short." Did you know that Fatmir Limaj was called Celiku? "A. Not in the beginning. When I knew him, I knew him as Celiku. Afterwards I learned his name as well." A little bit further on: "Q. But when he arrived with the group in Switzerland you didn't know his name at that time, in March, in 1998? "A. No, I didn't know the name. "Q. If you look on page 7 of that transcript at the top, you've got the question from the interviewer of the Limaj Defence team. "Q. You said you had known Fatmir. With what nickname did you know him?" Answer from General Selimi: "A. I knew Fatmir with the nickname Celiku."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You said page 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the pagination on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've got a document looking quite different from the one you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm talking about the English transcript of the questioning of the witness by the Defence team in October 2004. Now, although the questioning, as I said, was not clear at that particular part of testimony yesterday, what is clear is the witness was adamant that he wasn't sure when he learnt the name Celiku, which name he learnt first, and in every prior statement he has given regarding Fatmir Limaj's nickname, it has always been Celiku. Another area of contention, and I'm now up to page 6 of the chart which I've provided you of the differences in testimony yesterday and prior statements, that is the document Your Honour was holding up earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We have the issue of Fatmir Limaj as the commander of the Celiku units who were operating in the Pastrik zone adjacent to the witness's Drenica zone in May 1998. On the transcript on page 39 -- in the trial transcript the witness stated in answer to the witness stated in answer to the question "Which units -- on the other side of the road, which units operated? "A. On the other side of the road there were no formations. There were some units, Celiku -- some units named Celiku, which at that time started being organised. But they were working independent of each other." Later on I asked the witness specifically at page 47 of the transcript: "Who was the commander of the Celiku units in the battle for Lapusnik gorge in May 1998?" And the witness answered: "It's clear, I explained it earlier where the units acted. The units did not -- the units that existed did not act on the other side, they did not have a commander. They were independent and acted -- were acting independently." Further down he says: "The units, as I said, were not uniform, did not have a commander." And again, further down on page 7 of my chart: "So at the time the units acted as independent ones." This is clearly a material issue and one in which in previous statements the witness's answers have been different. On the right side of the page, 6, we have the transcript from page 32 and 33 of the transcribed Prosecution interview with the witness in 2003. On pages 32 to 33, as indicated, questioning about when Fatmir Limaj arrived from abroad in March 1998. Did he come to your area first?" The question was put to the witness. A little further down the witness stated: "I don't know exactly if he was based in Klecka. The General Staff was also based in Klecka at that time and Fatmir himself wanted that also because he was from that area. He had connections there and knew the territory." And then the witness stated: "Naturally he had some directive in the General Staff to create the units operating with other Celiku units." Now, on page 7, continuing: "Did you as commander, did you have direct communication with Fatmir Limaj about these issues, about the gorge, about Lapusnik?" Again concentrating on this time period. And the witness stated, "No we didn't get out orders from the General Staff." The witness has previously explained that the hierarchy was the General Staff, the zone commanders or area commanders like himself, and below that the units. Further down on page 8 of the chart --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interject. I'm trying to restrain myself. It's not clear what my friend is trying to do. Your Honour, my friend is simply going through reams of documents that's now being condensed before you, somewhat. But, Your Honours, that's hardly, in my submission, the way one seeks to make a witness adverse. And Your Honour, of course, later on -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. It is, I've got to confess for my own part, a little difficult to follow everything you're putting, Mr. Nicholls. utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The precise point of difference is not always easy to pick up as you go through it. utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to be clear on that. The first point I was making is that there is a strong and clear discrepancy on which order and when the witness knew Fatmir Limaj by different names. In previous interviews it's been very clear that he first knew the witness [sic] as Celiku, as Commander Celiku of the Celiku units and some months later learnt that this person named Celiku, who was the commander of the Celiku unit, had the real name of Fatmir Limaj. That was point one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Point one, to which I would put in the additional [inaudible] given by the witness by way of clarification, that from March 1998 he knew the accused by the name Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. He did know the name Celiku. However, what is different is that he stated earlier that he knew him as a Commander Celiku and that he did not even know this person's name was Fatmir Limaj. And in previous interviews the only nickname he's ever referred to was Celiku.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, an additional nickname comes in, but has the nickname Celiku ever been disavowed by the witness as one he knew that from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, just when he was -- it's the original point, and that is -- That is not the most important point of discrepancy; however, it is a relevant point. The second point which I've been talking about, more importantly, is who was in command of the Celiku units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In the time frame from -- starting with May 1998. The witness testified in court yesterday, stating twice these units in May 1998 during the battle for Lapusnik gorge had no commander. That was his testimony. In prior statements --

utterances.text: And at what point of time was that answer directed to?

utterances.text: May 1998. The question at page 47: "Who was the commander of the Celiku units in the battle for Lapusnik gorge on May" - and I think it's left out May 9th - "1998?" Is what I actually said. It says on May 1998 in the transcript. And then the answer is again: They had no commander. In the previous section of transcript I've pointed out where he knew the name Celiku, he knew him in the first couple of months, which would have been this period, as the Celiku, Commander of the Celiku units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where does that appear? Are you referring to the top of 7?

utterances.text: That appears at -- that should be on page 37, Your Honours. It's on page 37, the Prosecution's transcript of our interview with him.

utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I'm reading it plural. There are other statements that would indicate plural that I will get to. And there were, of course, multiple Celiku units. If you continue to page 10 of the --

Yeah, lower. "A. I didn't know anyone of the command structure around that area except for Fatmir, whose name I knew. I didn't know anyone else in that area." Below that from interview -- from our interview, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prosecution's interview, on page 40. The interviewer tries to clarify this issue. "Q. And the witness says: "Sorry?" And the question then is: "Q. Okay. The only name and position he knows about in the Celiku unit is that Fatmir Limaj was a commander." And the witness says: "Fatmir, and Kumanova's name as well. But I didn't know him. I had only seen him once." So again, there the witness affirms that Fatmir Limaj was the commander of the Celiku units. On page 11 of the chart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I could ask you to pause again, please. I'm both absorbing and noting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I raised this yesterday. This is behind tab 18 of your binders. It's the article given in 2000 by the witness, interview in Zeri. On page 12 of that interview in English we see the translation in English stating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, this was an interview with a journalist. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. A lengthy -- multi-part interview. And on page 12 the heading for this section is: "How and why we closed the Lapusnik gorge." On page 13 the interviewer asks the question: "Q. The battle for the gorge of Lapusnik presents one of the key moments of the war. What was the contribution of your units -- of the units of your zone in this battle?" The witness goes on to talk about the significance of the battle of 9 May in exactly -- this has to be the battle of 9 May because later on in the article they talk about the Serb offensive and the -- towards the end of July, where the gorge was lost. And the significance which the witness describes in the article to this battle is the same as he described in court yesterday, that of opening you have an arterial highway for the KLA to use. And the witness stated, in answer to the question by the interviewer, that these soldiers belonged to the 113 and the 121st Brigades and stated: "The units of the future 121 Brigade led by their Commander Celiku, Fatmir Limaj, were operating on the other side." Now, that's exactly what he said yesterday, except that when he spoke yesterday they were under -- operating under nobody's command, these units which would become part of the 121st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this isn't in the chart, but referring to the transcript of the interview which the witness gave to representatives of the Defence last year in October 2004. If you look at page 5 of that transcript, Your Honours. The third question asked of the witness on page 5 is: "What was his area of operation when he joined the KLA? What were his tasks?" Now, in context, it's clear that the question is referring to Fatmir Limaj. The previous question asks when the witness met Fatmir. And I won't read the whole answer but part of the answer is: "At this point when Fatmir came in Drenica, Fatmir went to the area where he was born, and was involved in the creation of fire positions, where there were several people or groups, like Celiku 1, 2, or 3." And it states "and ex-Celiks." But this was this period when I was zone commander. He exercised his responsibility in Pastrik. Now again, other than having a responsibility in this zone, it's the same as the testimony yesterday: that he came and went to the area where he was -- to that area, but not that he was -- set up these units and had a responsibility in the Pastrik zone on the other side of the road. The last question asked on the page, 5: "But these units, as you call them, Celiku 1, 2, 3, did you know more how they operate and act? Who is in charge of those positions?" And the witness states: "I don't know how they operated because I had another responsibility. The responsibility where I was commander and the brigades that existed in the Drenica zone were divided by the line of responsibility. The line of responsibility with Fatmir, or the operating zone, was the asphalt road starting from Komorane, near Klina," and then he talks again about the 121st Brigade. So he speaks of that road there as the dividing line of the responsibility with Fatmir Limaj at this time period when the Celiku 1, 2, 3 units are created after Fatmir Limaj has come back from the west, which, contextually, puts it in the March/May 1998 period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, the last issue I'll highlight are disciplinary measures. There was a long exchange on pages 29 to 34, about five pages of transcript, on this issue. And after a lot of questioning and going around the houses and some difficulty - and I'm talking here now pages 12 to 17 of the chart - the witness stated that it was possible that a soldier would be told to leave the unit and that they could be removed. That was after a great deal of, in my view and in my submission, efforts on his part to resist answering the question. If you contrast to that on page 12 of my chart, which refers to pages 44 and 45 of the interview, the taped interview which Mr. Selimi gave to the Office of the Prosecution, he's asked a quite simple question: "Q. So what would happen if there was a fight between soldiers or if a soldier left his post? What sort of disciplinary measures were available to you." The witness responds: "A. The team commander, the company commander, could report it and the brigade commander could decide. At that time we were not prepared for it -- for the experience, and in other words, we had to learn by trial and error." The next question was: "Q. So what, for example, if somebody did something really bad, something more than a fight? Could you discipline that person from the unit." And the answer was: "A. A lot of times, a lot of times that happened. And they take the weapons away from them and the uniform. That was the worst they could do, actually. They couldn't do anything else at the time. And I would say that you could never work for -- never be a member of the KLA again." So although that testimony ended up in the end consistent, I include that as an example of the witness's efforts to resist answering questions and to try not to give us the same information he's clearly stated earlier in his prior statements. We've passed out today a letter which I think the Court has already received. It's addressed to the Trial Chamber, sent by the witness on 23 November 2004, where he says he will not be a witness for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think it has been distributed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the first page in the bundle you have been taking us to is your analysis of the Prosecution interviews. We haven't seen it until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh. I include this letter, Your Honour, because there are two issues which are slightly different but they are related. The first is the witness is an adverse witness under the Rules which I practice on, as he aligned himself with the opposing party. That, clearly, the case with this witness. He's openly stated he did not want to come for us. Mr. Khan stated yesterday the witness refused to be a Prosecution witness; he's happy to be a Defence witness. He considers himself adverse to the Office of the Prosecutor. The second issue, besides -- and under the US rules of evidence 611, at that point I would be allowed to use leading questions if he was declared as adverse. In addition, though, the witness -- I think I've demonstrated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not in addition though. I don't believe we're at that point in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm just pointing out that he through this letter and through his statements when he was served with the subpoena to come here, he again said to the person serving him: I don't want to come. He obeyed the subpoena. He's adverse. He's an adverse witness. Through the examples I've shown Your Honours he's also a hostile witness, in that he's trying to avoid giving this information and he has given materially different statements on -- in court yesterday than he has in previous interviews to us, to the Defence, and to the press on important points. And there is a direct contradiction that it is a clear effort from him to try to avoid answering the question. So I think the law's fairly settled. I won't go into that now unless I have to, but I think we've met that burden and I ask that I be allowed to use leading questions and to put these prior statements to him. That's to clarify these points to allow him to explain any of these discrepancies. There's no lay jury here. It will allow the Court to better evaluate his evidence. And I can go more into that, but I think I've established that he's an adverse witness and a hostile witness in the legal in the meaning of that phrase. If the Court, after it considers this, feels that I have not reached that point, I ask leave as the questioning goes on to make that application again if there are more occasions where he divulges on material issues from statements he's made in prior interviews which are material issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we can indicate now that this application is made at this point in the evidence. If it should not succeed, there is nothing in the way of you renewing the application if something new emerges as it progresses. So you don't need leave. Is that the end of your submission, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you a volunteer, Mr. Topolski?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was turning to Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm a volunteer. We submit this application is without both foundation or merit. We submit that Your Honours can, absent as we understand it any jurisprudence arising from this Tribunal on the point, safely adopt the principle that adverse means hostile and not merely unfavourable. In indicating that is the principle we invite you to apply, we be no means concede in that that position has been arrived at here or indeed anywhere near it. We hope it might be of assistance to make one or two submissions, as it were, to place this application in context. We submit context is important. For a consideration of the context, we'll culminate in a submission as to what ought to have been the course here without ever having got to this pass. First of all, this is in the shape of this witness a KLA commander of considerable seniority. He comes to us today as a serving general in the KPC. And it is in the light of that that we invite the Court to read the last sentence of the letter written on his behalf indicating his lack of preparedness to give evidence, for the reason he gives for that displays, in our submission, as we read the words, no animus; still less hostility to the Office of the Prosecutor, but is rather a recognition of the delicate position in which historically and today he finds himself. He -- this is the third matter of context -- as we are told by Mr. Nicholls yesterday, and we agree with him, is the only witness interviewed by any Defence team who specifically requested the attendance of the OTP during the interview. That of itself another indicator, we submit, of a position very far from animosity towards the party calling him. He made no signed statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. He was the subject of a subpoena compelling his attendance, having written the letter or it having been written on his behalf at the back-end of last November. Nonetheless, notwithstanding all of those matters, they chose to call him, to set up this skittle in order to knock it down. There was from 1946 a precedent they could have adopted, the medical case, this Nuremburg case. They could have invited the Tribunal to call the witness, had they feared what they now say has come about. And given the context, given the history and given the personality that we are dealing with here, it may be thought by the Tribunal that that would have been an application that would have found some favour. Can I turn from the context to what happened yesterday and make these submissions. First of all, it must be important to recognise, as with all witnesses who come before this or indeed any other court anywhere else in the world: If they are not speaking or being asked questions in their own language, in other words through an interpreter, there are potential difficulties in that fact alone. But like any witness, we submit, this witness would and would continue to benefit from being asked clear, concise, and precise questions. It is with regret that, we submit, there are examples throughout the examination-in-chief yesterday when that was not the case. May I give an example of a question that, on my account, contains four questions within one. Page 13 of the uncorrected transcript, line 3. "Q. And why would he have contact with the General Staff, what was the nature, what would the General Staff tell him to do or what was -- what was the reason for these contacts?" Four questions in one. To which the answer from this witness who's now characterised as having animus: "I hope it's a question for the members of the General Staff and not for me." We submit that questions of that kind and questions in a leading form has been a feature of this examination-in-chief thus far to the extent that it was only as a result of the intervention from the Court did we achieve any understandable clarity at all regarding the meeting with Limaj, whose case, as I've understood it for the last six weeks, has never been to dispute that he is Celiku. An example of a leading question on a matter of some controversy is, as Mr. Nicholls well knows, when the brigades were created and by whom is of some importance in this case when one looks at the issue of armed conflict. And at page 39 this is the question: "Now, on the 9th of May, 1998, you probably remember that date. What was going on with the 113 Brigade, the Pellumbi units, starting then in their zone?" Whatever I think that question, means it presupposes there was a 113 Brigade on the 19th [sic] of May, and that is very much an issue for this Court to decide. We submit that however careful a textual analysis we've been presented with this afternoon, however carefully that is done, of course when somebody's giving statements to the press, or interviews to others, a detailed textual analysis is going to throw up inconsistencies of one or another. But Mr. Nicholls gave the game away, we submit, when he took you to page 12 and said of the interviewer's question that he was asked quite a simple question. And look what the simple question was: "What would happen if there was a fight between soldiers or a soldier left his post? What sort of disciplinary measures were available to you?" That question generates an answer. It's a simple, clear, concise, precise question. That's been the problem here, we submit; not an attitude of animus or hostility to the Prosecution. The application to cross-examine him, because that's really what Mr. Nicholls is asking to do now, to cross-examine him on the newspaper interview in a sense puts the cart before the horse because as yet there is no evidence that that interview is an accurate record of what was said. And that is certainly a hurdle over which Mr. Nicholls would have to climb or jump, were he, in our submission, to be entitled in the first place as a matter of first principles to put a newspaper interview to a witness. Your Honours, that, we submit, is the context; that, we submit, is the position as indicated in those submissions; and that is why we put it as high at the outset of our reply as saying that this submission, this application, is both without foundation or merit and should fail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was not on the air. I think Mr. Topolski, and I call on you, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hopefully will not repeat the submissions that have been made by my learned friend. But in my submission, and whilst I don't mean it personally, I have the greatest of affection for my learned friend, we have wasted more than an hour of valuable court time. Your Honour, we on this side of your bench are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. making every effort to expedite this trial as far as possible. Only this morning we had meetings with the Prosecution agreeing a whole raft of expert witnesses. We are not belabouring any point, we hope, when witnesses are before you. And in that context trying to keep the ball rolling, trying to get to a fair determination of this matter, it does cause me, unfortunately, Your Honours, discomfort to say that the submission that my learned friend made has been frivolous and it has been utterly devoid of merit. Indeed, Your Honours, under the Rules you had power, if anybody on this side of the bench would dare to make such an uninformed and baseless submission, to direct that our legal fees not be paid. Your Honour, the application has been made. And once again a slur has been cast against a senior official of Kosova. Now, Your Honour, of course there are many witnesses who may hold my client in high esteem. You will remember the opening, perhaps, given by my learned friend Mr. Mansfield and the statements made by various internationals, head of the OSCE, head of Democratisation, the prime minister of Kosova. It may be that other witnesses who come to this court say good things about Mr. Limaj. Your Honour, if the Prosecution wish to call those witnesses as witnesses of truth, they must take the consequences. But to seek to allege that a general of the TMK operating under UN auspices is not a man of his word - and the Prosecution have said today that he has changed his story. To a man in uniform, that is to call him a liar. And, Your Honour, I do take exception to this unnecessary attempt by the Prosecution to impugn the credibility of their own witness simply because, with the greatest of respect, they have failed, due to very inartful and rather confused examination-in-chief, to get evidence out of him that they wanted. But, Your Honour, the Prosecution have utterly failed, in my submission, to show any hostile animus on the part of the witness that has appeared before you. The witness has been contacted a number of times by the Prosecution. Your Honour, on the 19th of November of 2003 he was interviewed. You have that before you. He again was interviewed on the 4th of May of last year, and the Prosecution had some technical problems and lost that interview; it wasn't recorded. And the notes also I think were not up to much. And, Your Honour, the Prosecution were present when the Defence spoke to that witness, both on the 11th of October, 2004, and again on Sunday. He is here before you. Now, Your Honour, some cultural sensitivity is required in any international trial, civil or criminal. Many of these witnesses come from a civil-law system in which ownership of witnesses is not known. The concept of a Prosecution witness or a Defence witness is something alien to them. And, Your Honour, your brothers in previous cases have encountered that. And in fact I think it was in the Blaskic case it was decided in at least one decision, and perhaps it has been overturned, but once a witness comes to court, he's a Court witness. And, Your Honour, that's what the witness was seeking to clarify yesterday, and, Your Honour, in my submission, that was clarified and he sought to answer every question honestly. Indeed, Your Honour, you will remember before he left the room yesterday at the Prosecution's own invitation or application, he again said, "I am willing to explain." Your Honour, this can hardly be consistent with a man that is seeking to obfuscate and not tell the truth. Your Honour, I cannot even say that the discrepancies are more apparent than real. In my submission, the discrepancies are nonexistent. I rather feel, unfortunately, like the young boy who shouted out: "The emperor has no clothes." But Your Honour, when I look at the alleged discrepancies, that's how I do feel. Because all this, in my submission, if not baloney, this distraction about the name Celiku, the witness was quite candid that he knew Mr. Limaj as Celiku. He can't remember his name in 1996. He remembers his name from 1998 but he can't seem to remember - and this is where questioning is so important - he can't remember the first time he was introduced what he was introduced as. Well, in my submission, besides everything else, how is that relevant? How is that relevant? Was that really necessary to justify so much of our precious court time? Your Honour, once again, and we see plenty of examples of leading in this court, and as Mr. Mansfield said with the previous witness, he's stopped or he's very slow to object now on the basis of leading questions. But of course at that leading-type of question pollutes also the interview process. Your Honour, at page 35 of the Prosecution interview, the witness is asked about the name Celiku's units -- the name Celiku units and, in my submission, gives a very honest answer: "I don't know. I don't know where they got the name from. Maybe Celiku means something strong. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I don't know." Now, Your Honour, when the Prosecution investigator seeks to say later on, well, are you talking about Mr. Fatmir's units, of course you will judge for yourselves the relevance of that. But a witness may speculate and he may also testify as to core evidence that he knows. And many times, many a time, in my submission, difficulties are encountered when a witness is asked to deviate from what he knows and enter the uncertain and dangerous realm of speculation. And on repeated occasions, both in interview and here whilst the witness is in the box, witnesses are invited to engage upon this task of speculation. And, Your Honour, that's another problem that has been encountered. Your Honour, my learned friend touched upon the absurdity of the comments about newspaper article. It's not for us, with the greatest of respect, to tell the Prosecution how to prosecute. It is very basic when it comes to this newspaper article. There's no journalist before you. The witness has not even been asked by Mr. Whiting [sic] whether or not every word of that interview is a true record of his conversation with the journalist, and he is seeking to impugn the credibility of his witness on the basis of the witness's unadopted, unverified and untested interview with a newspaper. Your Honour, again, hardly the basis, hardly the solid legal foundation that could eat up so much of your precious court time. Your Honour, when it comes to the disciplinary measures - this is my final point, because you will make up your own minds when it comes to the witness - Your Honour, in page 44 of his interview he's asked about the disciplinary measures that were available to him at the time, and of course he described the fact that the Drenica unit was at a more advanced side of evolution than other units. His answer, in my submission, again is not inconsistent of the tenor of what he said yesterday. He said at the top of page 45 in fact: "At the time we were not prepared for it. We were not prepared for disciplinary measures. We were not prepared for the experience at all. In other words, we learnt by trial and error." And, Your Honour, then of course he does say that weapons can be taken away and people can be dismissed, but that's exactly what he said yesterday. Now, it may not all be served up on a silver platter by Mr. Whiting -- to Mr. Nicholls, but the question is when is the witness is asked a specific question, he answers truthfully and consistently. Your Honour, for those reasons and many others it's my submission that the application, with the greatest of respect, is frivolous and is devoid of merit and indeed should be summarily rejected. Your Honour, unless I can assist, those are my - I've tried to be brief - submissions on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that in large measure the difficulty with Mr. Nicholls' application is a failure of the art of the questions that he has asked thus far, as opposed to the substantive answers that have been given by the witness. And since Mr. Nicholls suggested yesterday that we practice in the same jurisdiction and that I would share his thoughts with regard to how this witness is treated, I would unfortunately have to at this point say that Mr. Nicholls has unfortunately taken my name in vain, because with regard to his performance, and by that I mean the kinds of questions asked this witness and the responses given, in the courts in which I practice, this application would be denied based upon what he has done thus far. With regard to the issue of this gentleman's demeanour, I find it curiously strange that he would be in any sense whatsoever characterised or defined hostile. We've actually had an example of a witness who exhibited some hostility towards questioners in this court, and that was Mr. Safiulin who engaged in banter with us, and as a matter of fact you could say was pugilistic in some of his responses. Such is not the case with this witness; as a matter of fact to the contrary: In one situation where he was presented with a map that failed to have sufficient information on it for him to give the Prosecutor that which he desired, he attempted on his own to worry through the document and point out the very fact for which the Prosecutor was looking. With regard to issues concerning, for example, discipline - and now I refer to the very page that you've been referred to before - the Prosecutor did not seek or elicit information on page 44 of their interview at the top of the page when their investigator asks: "Q. What were the duties of the military police?" And he responds: "A. The main one was to discipline soldiers inside, but sometimes, Inakovic [phoen], for example, they also keep law and order. So" -- several words were unintelligible. But that did not happen very often cause -- since we were always on attack, on the defensive. We had to move a lot of times. So they mostly," - referring to the military police - "they were busy with the wounded and they took them and they transported them, and so on." That answer was not sought. That answer, as a matter of fact, was not given. Is the failure of him to give such information in these proceedings, based upon the questions that were given to him by Mr. Nicholls, such that you would define him as being hostile? I think not. In sum, the application is without merit and should be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, any response.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll be very brief, Your Honour. It's settled in this Tribunal in the case law Brdjanin and Talic case, the Blagojevic case, that a party calling a witness may treat a witness as hostile. Hostility does not mean in anger, hostility in the normal sense of the word. Hostility can normally be demonstrated simply by changing their statements from ones which the party calling them reasonably expect them to rely on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it too concise to say that it's a witness who's not prepared to answer truthfully and willingly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Quite right, Your Honour, or who is not prepared to answer with a great deal -- will take every step possible to avoid answering the question; and then, you're right, will not alter or answer truthfully in line with prior statements. Mr. Topolski's made the point, it's a bit contradictory, that the witness did cooperate with us, did allow us to go to his interview with the Defence, and has expressed all along that he was willing to come here and testify but he did not want to be called by the Prosecutor. Based on that I think we're entitled to expect that when he comes to testify he will say the same things as he's said consistently in his interviews. The magazine article, the newspaper article, is not the be-all and end-all, but it's consistent with the thrust of the other statements. The name issue, paragraph 26 of Mr. Limaj's Defence brief states, his pre-trial brief, that: "Mr. Limaj, when he came to Klecka soon gained the nickname "Daja," uncle, in Albanian, as well as a previous nickname "Arben." Whilst it is true that Fatmir Limaj was also later known as Celiku, he gained that name because it was the call sign of one of the units that was subsequently formed. He did not give his name to some of the units nor were they named." I just raise that to show that that issue was not entirely without dispute from the Defence side. Finally, we did not call this witness to knock him down. I am not attempting to slur -- to cast any slurs. What I -- the purpose of this application is to be allowed to use leading questions to show the witness his prior statements, allow him to explain to the Chamber these discrepancies, and there are, I think I'm demonstrated, some marked discrepancies on material issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that the application should be refused. The issue which we are to consider is, commonly put, whether or not the witness should be declared hostile. The essence of a hostile witness is usually regarded as one who is not prepared to speak the truth. That can be by simply refusing to answer or by giving false testimony or withholding relevant information. And the submissions of Mr. Nicholls suggest that on some views of prior statements, that view could be taken of aspects of the present evidence in this hearing of the witness. The matters that have been identified by Mr. Nicholls each bear a possible interpretation which supports the application. We, therefore, are not of the same view of the application as was advanced by at least one counsel for the Defence. It is not without possible merit. But the matters that have been identified are not such, in our view, as to persuade us that the view ought to be taken that this witness is hostile in the sense that I have identified. Of the matters that have been referred to, the reference on meeting in May 1998 to the name "Celiku" was certainly confused; the clarification in the end, however, was in relatively straightforward terms. And apart from the possible refinement that there may have been an actual introduction by another name or even two potentially different names, the end result was that it was Celiku and that was, as we would understand it, exactly the point of the previous statement that was relied upon in this connection. So there appeared no material distinction in the end on the point. There certainly is and there apparently remains a difference between the evidence of the witness given here as to the units fighting on the southern side of the Pristina-Pec road and those fighting on the north, as to their leadership. This is anything but a straightforward issue, though, both in the way the questioning was conducting in this hearing and the way in which the questions and the answers proceeded in each of the previous statements to which we've been referred. Difficulties clearly exist in time frames, in that the organisation of units and their eventually becoming so-called brigades appears to have been progressive over the relevant period. And the most critical reference that most apparently supports Mr. Nicholls' submission refers to the area in which the future 121st Brigade functioned, and that, as far as the Chamber presently understands, was a brigade that was commanded by Celiku. And the question of which time sense these various references intended when they speak to earlier units or points which came in the end to comprise or be part of the 121st Brigade. Without going through each of them individually at this point, it's sufficient to say that there is uncertainty about that as the Chamber reads the evidence. Sufficient to leave it at the moment unclear whether the difference is due to some reasonably simple explanation or is a change of position absolutely on the part of the witness. But whatever the answer to that may be - and we have no means of knowing that at the moment - we are left without a view that this is motivated by a hostility in the relevant sense. The matter of disciplinary measures was the only other significant distinction, and the end position reached, admittedly with difficulty, appears to be exactly the same as in the previous statements. For those reasons, the Chamber is not persuaded that there would be justification for treating the witness at the present time at hostile to the Prosecution. Given the time, this would appear to be an appropriate time for the first break, and we will resume at -- I guess precisely 10 past, but we seem to have difficulty getting precision in all the various aspects of this organisation coming together at a precise moment. But we will live in hope at 10 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. Thank you for your patience in waiting. We've resolved the difficulties and we are ready to continue with the evidence that you give to this Tribunal. Could I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence; it still applies. Now Mr. Nicholls has some more questions before counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to try to continue asking you some questions where we left off yesterday. And I also apologise for the delay of the time you've had to wait probably in a rather small room outside the courtroom. At one point yesterday we were talking about the Lapusnik battle of May 9th, 1998. Do you remember we were discussing that battle?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. It's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You began talking about the significance of that battle for the KLA, what that battle achieved strategically. Could you expand on that a little bit. What you said yesterday was you were talking about how there is now a free corridor for transporting weapons. I'd ask you to explain a little bit more how that corridor was used and why it was important.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I explained it yesterday but I can tell it again today. This was because our movement and the supply of weapons and the circulation of citizens -- because all citizens were isolated and they were in other parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you describe the types of weapons or munitions that you were able to bring in or that were transported now down this corridor?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were mainly light weapons which you could carry on -- on your shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in addition to weapons, was any ammunition for those weapons transported in along this corridor which had been opened up?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is normal then when we took weapons, they were taken together with ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly can you describe where these ammunition and weapons came from. Where did they originate?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were -- got supplies mainly from the motherland, Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the ammunition which came from Albania, can you tell me what manufacturer that was, where it had been manufactured prior to you obtaining it?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they were manufactured, but we got supplies, as I said, from Albania. They were the weapons coming from Albania, from the Albanian state, the Albanian citizens, which we used at the time. But we had also weapons that were used and we also used weapons of a Yugoslav manufacture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And the last question on this, I'm just trying to be clear. You say Albanian weapons and ammunition. Does that mean that these were munitions or weapons actually manufactured in Albania?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were of an Albanian -- manufactured in Albania or in China.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You also spoke about the free movement or the circulation of citizens once this corridor had been opened. Can you describe a little bit -- expand on what you mean by that and why that's important.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was important because we were limited. People needed various things, the elementary basics of -- to make a living.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, after the May 9th battle, how long did the KLA forces remain in control of the corridor or this arterial road?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I cannot tell you exactly how long. It was a long period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you give me an estimate in months, weeks?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I don't know because very often the Serbian forces moved and it was completely blocked. So I don't know how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, towards -- excuse me for my voice. Towards late July, 25th July, can you describe what military operations were occurring, if any, in the Lapusnik gorge zone?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You have no memory of that at all?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date of 25th July -- I cannot recall the date, not because on the 25th but also during 1998 and 1999 I was operating in the zone of Drenica. I was in the operational zone of Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, once this road had been opened, or corridor, after 9th of May, which units on the Drenica side -- did any units of the Drenica side participate in defending the road after 9 May?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they acted as units, as I explained yesterday. The Guri units, Alpha, and Pellumbi units have acted at the time. This was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at this point after 9th of May, you've already described yesterday the Drenica zone, the boundary of the Drenica zone being the Tarmac highway, the Pristina-Pec highway. Does that continue to be the boundary zone after 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the beginning, at the end, we, this was within the operational -- the boundary zone of the operational zone of Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, on other side of the road in the Pastrik zone, what units operated after 9th of May, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Celiku units operated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was their responsibility, if any, with regard to the road which formed the northern border of their zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units were not linked to each other and they were not normally along the road. They were also operating in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. What I'm asking you -- I'll try again. Which units on that side were responsible for the road?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because this area did not belong to me, but I know that they were the Celiku units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What communication was there between units of these two different zones regarding the road or security for the road after 9 May 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units communicated with each other as they could, either with radio communication or, if they were close to each other, they communicated in various ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you could please give us some examples of the types of issues that they would have communicated about. What was important for them to talk about regarding that road which formed the boundary between the zones?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding this road, I do not know the types of issue they talked. But in general, if a village was attacked somewhere by the Serbian forces, then we coordinated with each other in order to come to the help of this village. As for the Lapusnik gorge, all the units that were on my -- under my control, the majority of the units went to help their -- as regards the Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You also stated yesterday that this road, the Pristina-Pec road, had been used by the Serb forces to mount attacks on civilians. Is that -- do I remember that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Once this road had been secured by yours forces and the Celiku units on the other side, what steps were taken to monitor traffic on the road?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has never been blocked, as it was said, because the Serbian forces very often managed to penetrate there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. But you've explained that this was an important road and the road was used for movement of civilians and ammunition. Now, during the time that the road is under the control of the KLA after May 9th, is there any effort made to monitor what is going up and down that road? Isn't it -- would that be important?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not that important because the road was free. And then we tried to get consolidated and to deal more with the brigades, with improvement of infrastructure and the -- operate the other operational zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So is your -- if I understand -- Well, the road itself, the actual Pristina-Pec highway, who was responsible for the road and traffic on the road? Was that your units on the Drenica side or the Celiku units on the other side?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Both units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was any part of that responsibility control of traffic, in other words, seeing who and what was being moved up and down that road?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I cannot recall because it was a period of units. But my soldiers who were under the area of responsibility were told not to go to the other side or not to go to the other side without first getting permission by official persons or commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who would grant that permission or permits on your side?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were the units, and of course it was normal for the commander of the unit to give such an order, such a permit. The person in charge of the units. This was as long as the units existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me go back now to another topic you were talking about yesterday, and that was your meeting with Fatmir Limaj after he returned from the west in 1998. Do you remember we were beginning to talk about that?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When he came back in 1998 and you met him, you stated that he was at that point a soldier, whereas in 1996 he had been a student. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met him as a student in 1996, where in 1998 I met him for the first time as a soldier in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And tell me again if you can when it was in 1998 that you met him as a soldier in uniform.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime after March, after the tragic events of the fall of the legendary commander. It was probably after April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, can you describe just briefly your relationship to Mr. Limaj? I mean your personal relationship, how you consider him, what terms you were on with him normally.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the period I met him --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From when you met him until today.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I met him, I met him as a -- he was an unknown person to me and as a soldier. During the war, I met him as a soldier first on the other side and then later as Commander Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell me -- what do you mean you met him as a soldier first on the other side?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "the other side," this is because the first time we met he was on the other side in Klecka or on that side, on that area where he was born, on the Berisa side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be clear, that's on the other side of the Pristina-Pec highway in the Pastrik zone?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I mean is: Now, today, how do you consider Mr. Limaj? As a friend? As a colleague? Can you describe how you feel about this man.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have respect for him, for Limaj, and all the members of the KLA. And all those who are present here such as Isak Musliu and Haradin Bala. I have represent for all those who fought and shed their blood for the Kosovo Liberation Army. I have the same respect for Fatmir Limaj as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell me after you met him in 1998 when he returned where he went next, where he was assigned as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said previously, and you said it, when he went to the other side, other part of Berisa -- and his stay was -- he can explain it better here. But as far as I know he was in the nearby villages and I think it was in Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, he, you stated, became a commander. What was his first point of command? Can you tell us, from your knowledge and from what you know about his military career after he arrived, where did he -- what assignments did he carry out?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What assignments and what responsibility he had you can ask him himself. I can reply -- give you answers here only about my responsibility. As far as I can remember this was at the time when he was commander of the 121st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when did he assume that command?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Approximately?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I do not err, it might have been September 1998 or October. I cannot tell it for sure. Probably it was the end of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And before he assumed the command of the 121st Brigade, what were his duties? Who was he command -- what was his role then?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him at the time simply as Celiku and as Fatmir in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which area?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "that area," it's implied, it means the area or Berisa. We can call it the operational zone of Pastrik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the Celiku units in May and June 1998 -- you've stated that there was some communication regarding the road between the Pellumbi units on your side and the Celiku units.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this was the zone adjacent to you, your zone. Who was commander of the Celiku units in May and June 1998? And could I ask what you're looking at? You've taken out some papers, for the record.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the transcripts when I've given my first statement and which also you have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And would you like to use those to refresh your memory? Is that why you've taken them out, to help you remember?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no need for this because it is clear to me. However, if I don't remember anything then I might have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would help the Chamber, General - and you understand you're giving the evidence for this Chamber so that we can learn what happened - it would help us if we heard your recollection, your memory, first. If you don't remember a particular matter and would like to refer to some original record of yours or statement, indicate that and then we can know whether that's your present memory or something you may have remembered earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now then I'll ask you: Do you remember now who commanded the Celiku units in May, June, and July 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units, as long as they were units, no one commanded those units. Each had a responsibility in those units and the units were separated. I said it yesterday, and I have not said this in the transcript before. I'm saying it now just to argue, to give you arguments, that the units were independent of each other. And starting from my logic when I operated in this area, this means that on the other side the units were independent of each other. There has not been a commander, someone who commanded the unit or someone who was a -- who had command about these units -- over these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You say in your answer that you said it yesterday and you've not said it in the transcripts before. Why haven't you said that in the transcripts before when you've been interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps it can be asked what he means the transcript before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue with your question, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You may answer the question, General.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm answering this question exactly. I would like to dwell on this point more elaborately, if I'm allowed to. When I received the first summon by the Prosecution -- by the Prosecutor Carla Del Ponte, it was about giving the person -- my personal data, the military career, and the activity of the KLA in 1998 and 1999. And Mr. Ole Lehtinen was the Prosecution -- the investigator. At the time, they asked me to be interviewed by them. I don't know whether Mr. Lehtinen is present here. He asked me when I was available to be interviewed. And you can -- he said, You can -- do you want to be interviewed today or do you want to be interviewed tomorrow? I agreed to be interviewed tomorrow, and the next day I gave that statement or was interviewed. The reason is that it was not clearly defined because it was the activity during 1998 and 1999 and this included a lot of things. And when it came to the Lapusnik gorge or the units, I've said it and it's here in the transcript. Even when we will discuss now, I've talked about the Celiku units if I'm saying it clear. I've said things about the camp and the units. But this -- they did not -- for some of the things they did not remind me -- they did not ask me at that moment. And the fresh recollection of my memory, because it was 1998 and 1999 and it was a long period and I was not prepared. I just told them what they asked me. I'm sorry. To continue. And given the fact that I did not give arguments yesterday was that because I've solemnly declared here to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And at the time I could not remember a lot of things, many things related to that period that they did not remind me of or they did not ask me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your testimony, then, to make sure I understand you clearly what you've just explained, is that you did not state in your interview with the Prosecutor that the Celiku units had no -- were all independent units without a commander because you were not asked that question? You weren't asked about that or you didn't remember at the time?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is what I've said, and we can show it here. If you can have a look at the transcript, even check the words that I've said - and you have it in front of you and I have it in front of me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like you to take me, please, to the part of the transcript you're referring to, if you could.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is tab 19, probably the middle of tab 19, when it says: "Do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you know who was the commander of the forces on the other side of the road under the command of Fatmir Limaj?" And my answer is this, if you have it in front of you. Or my answer has been that. May I read it here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer has been as such: "No. In that part I've never known -- I don't know who has the responsibility, which means who has commanded a part -- except as Fatmir." When I say "except at Fatmir," I just want to say simply not as Celiku but simply as Fatmir, as a person whom I've known on that part which means that -- I have not said that he has commanded there or I have not said that he was responsible -- has commanded the units. However, I have said that I have known him in that part as Fatmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you give me the page number that you're reading from, if you're reading from the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's page 19. It's -- transcript is V000-4792.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court, I think we're at page 39 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Albanian translation is number 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you remember whether you ever said during these -- during this interview that Limaj was a commander, known as Celiku? That Celiku was a commander?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've said it and I'm saying it again now. I've said it even earlier that he was commander. I've known him as a commander of the 121st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at page 18 of your transcript, the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Khan. I think we may have a similar thought, but you better put yours first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hope it's similar. Your Honour, of course I trust that my friend will not seek to go behind the ruling that you made before the break. It seems that that is what he has, if not already done, what he is about to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And he was therefore going to be cautioned by me, and we're leading well into that. You realise that the witness has volunteered certain matters which you've been allowed so far to pursue, but you should pursue those as examination-in-chief and not by way of cross-examination. Now, if you want to you will be therefore under some restraint as you should proceed from this point in dealing with the past transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's just that the witness has now put the transcript in issue, explaining that the transcript reflects --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know what you mean, but you cannot ignore the restraints on your ability to deal with the situation because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just think that the situation is slightly different now because the witness has explained that in the transcript he has explained the issue of -- that he's talking about, the time and place of command. So I think it's a bit artificial to focus just on one spot in the transcript. The entirety of the transcript should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You might well ask the witness whether he said other things about that issue and what he said and what he meant by them. And subject to any objection as it progresses, as long as he is giving the evidence and you are merely ensuring that we have his full account of what he believes he said and what he meant, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's where I was starting to ask you, Witness, if you talked in other places in this transcript -- in your interview about Celiku's command.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have the transcript in front of you. It might be possible what you mean in other -- in other places, in the places where he was located or something else. You mean something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I mean is, General: Do you remember talking at other times during this interview which is in the transcript about Limaj's command, who he was in command of, which units?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, I do not recall. As far as I can recall -- because you remember when they gave the transcript to me and when you gave that subpoena. Even if I asked to have the transcript, it was not given to me. As far as I can remember when Fatmir went, went to the sight of the part of Berisa, where because he knew the area -- he knew the area there. However, as a commander I do not know. I know him only as a commander, Celiku. And I'm saying it again, I don't know -- I don't know and I've said it. If I eve said such a thing, then I can give you the clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you to explain, because it's not clear to me completely, your answer regarding the part of the transcript you read out. That was on page 19 of your version, on page 39 of the English. I'm going to ask you because I don't understand your answer completely. You were asked if you knew who was in command of the forces in Lapusnik on the other side of the road lower than Fatmir Limaj. And your answer was: "I didn't know of anyone of the command structure around that area except for Fatmir, whose name I knew. I didn't know anyone else in that area." Now, could you please explain what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear and I'm explaining it again. It is clear. Besides the only person whom I've known in that area and those units was Fatmir. However, I have not said that those units were -- Fatmir was in command of those units. Let us be clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you ever said -- have you ever described the units that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again I do object. This is clearly an attempt to go behind the decision that's already been made by Your Honours. The witness can be asked to describe Mr. Limaj's alleged command responsibility. He can be asked to describe the alleged structure of the KLA at the time, but that should be referenced to direct questions and direct answers rather than a transcript which is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You were, I believe, Mr. Nicholls, going down a wrong path at that moment. The objection was well-made. While you think next to go, would you excuse me for a moment if I intervene with the witness. General, you've told us that you first met the accused Fatmir Limaj as a soldier when he came again in 1998 to Kosovo. And you met him then as a soldier and you came to know him as Celiku. Later, as I understand your evidence, you learned that his name was Fatmir. Is that a correct understanding of your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A little while ago you mentioned that you knew him as Commander Celiku.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said I knew him as Commander Celiku because in the process of the formation of the units in Berisa or in the Pastrik operational zone with the formation of Brigade 121, I knew him as Commander Celiku. That was how I came to know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that you came to know him as Commander Celiku only in the course of the formation of the 121st Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how it is. After the brigade was formed I recognised him after some time as Commander Celiku, because fighting was going on and when the brigade was formed I was not present. I didn't know under what circumstances it was formed, that brigade. Therefore, I knew about him sometime in 1998. It was September, I think. I'm not very sure of the time when I heard of him as Commander Celiku.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you use the name Commander Celiku about him after that when speaking about him or to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When I've talked about him I have referred to him as Commander Celiku, but I think it's important the time when we have operated and when we have communicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him described as Commander Celiku before the formation of the 121st Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I have, as Commander Celiku, commander of point 1 or so. Because often every unit was referred to when they saw me as commander or another commander of war unit. In this context he was referred to as commander; that was before the formation of the brigade. And it is very likely I've heard about him in that context and it is very likely I've referred to him as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, is that referring to him as commander of one point or unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you, I'm not very sure how the organisation was in that area, what operated. But when I heard people say Commander Celiku, I knew it was Fatmir -- I knew it was Commander Celiku. It might be Commander Celiku number 1, number 2, but there were many Celiku units, as I said, which were in operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you had no detailed knowledge of those units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or of who was the individual commander of each of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, with exception of Fatmir whom I met first and I said to you and I explained to you earlier. I didn't know the other commanders of these other Celiku units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During the summer of 1998, May, June, and July, did you -- which period, as best you remember, did you know of Commander Celiku as commander of one of the Celiku units, Celiku 1 or one of the other units?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly at what period of time I got to know him as such. I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember stating that units you've talked about on one side of the road would communicate with units directly on the other side of the road?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was the Celiku 1 unit one of the units which units on your side of the road would have to communicate with during May, June, July 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They communicated with Celiku unit number 1, but also with other Celiku unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And when were they communicating with these Celiku units? During what period?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the need arose for that or when one of them asked for assistance, for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you recall any incidents then of communication with Commander Celiku during one of these communications for assistance?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the moment, I can't think of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During that period, May, June, and July, what was the main -- what were the main tasks of the Celiku units, of Celiku 1 and the other units?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How detailed is your knowledge of what operations were taking place on the other side of the road, other than this specific request for assistance?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not. I did not know what operations they were engaged in because I had to take care of my own responsibilities in my zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What operations, what activities, if you know, was Commander Celiku involved in in May, June, July 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'll have to ask you for your answer again. It wasn't picked up for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request the witness to stand closer to the mike, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, during the battle on May 9th in the Lapusnik gorge 1998, were the Celiku units - we talked about this yesterday - involved in that battle?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were involved in that battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was Commander Celiku, as commander of any of the Celiku units or in any other capacity, did he take part in that important battle?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But as far as I recall, yes, he took part in that battle. He may as well say it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell us as best you remember what part what he took in that battle. What actions did he take against the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what actions he undertook, but probably he has been there in his capacity as Fatmir or as a soldier of the KLA he has tried as best he could with his unit, like I did with my units, to contribute to that battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you remember in this battle against the Serb forces who relatively had a better position against the Serb forces, your units or the Celiku units on the other side?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
