utterances.text: My position -- I don't know how I can explain it to you. The position of Celiku units, they were closer to the enemy. We had better position in terms of operation, attacks. Regarding the concentration of forces, my forces were greater. Our operational zone had a larger number of forces. Several units of our operational zone in Drenica were involved in the Lapusnik gorge battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in particular, do you remember the position -- Commander Celiku's position? What kind of position he was in? What kind of advantage or disadvantage, how difficult it was for him in that battle?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: His strategic position was -- I don't know if you have an idea of Lapusnik gorge. So we -- both of us had taken positions. We were - when I say "we," I mean the Drenica operational zone units and the other units that operated there - both had taken their respective positions on the other side of the road. When I say the opposite side of the road, I mean the Berisa area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you remember during that battle who had the higher ground, your unit or Fatmir Limaj's unit?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by high ground. You mean in terms of position, strategic position?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a mountainous area.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Celiku units were closer to the road, but our units, too. When they operated in this part there were some of them, some units, that went to the rescue of Celiku units. I don't know how clear I am. But our units were mostly concentrated in Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, when you're talking about going to the rescue of Celiku units or any of those units commanded Commander Celiku, is that one of the units that you assisted or not?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Celiku did not have any commandeering position then, in that operation. As I said earlier, this brigade was in the process of formation. Even in my zone, when some units needed help, other units went to their rescue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The transcript states commander Celiku did not have any commandeering position. Is that what you -- can you clarify what you said for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me who was the commander as far as I understood you, I if got you right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You had earlier explained that at this period, in answer to some of the Court's questions if I'm correct, that Commander Celiku had the command of a unit, one of the Celiku units. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what I'm asking you is that during this May 9th battle you've talked about Fatmir Limaj's involvement. If you know, was his unit one of the ones that was aided or that your units communicated with or fought with?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not go to the rescue of Celiku's units. We went to help those units that were stationed near this area, Guri, Pellumbi, as I said. But usually normally during fighting it was possible for some units to help other units; that was not the case only with Celiku unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked about this being an important battle and that your view now of Fatmir Limaj is one of respect. Can you tell the Court how he acquitted himself in this battle, how his performance was.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Fatmir is best suited to answer this question. I don't know how he fought, what his performance was, because that was a very difficult moment. Villages were set fire to, inhabitants began to flee their homes. So I cannot tell you how he fought. I think it's up to Fatmir to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, at any time after 9 May were you involved in any combat operations together with units commanded by Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Part of the border of your zone of responsibility we saw on the map, the Pristina-Pec highway goes through the town of -- the village of Lapusnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you go yourself to Lapusnik during May, June, July 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the fighting broke out I did, but I wasn't able to penetrate into Lapusnik, only to Krekov [phoen], in the vicinity of Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know which units -- whether -- which units were responsible for Lapusnik on the other side of the highway, on the Pastrik zone side?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Celiku units were responsible for that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you remember, which Celiku units?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying it several times. I don't know how many other Celiku units existed. I know that there were several operating in that area, but I don't know how many and which they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, other than Fatmir Limaj, were there any other commanders named Celiku operating in that area, the other side of the Pristina-Pec highway, in May, June, July 1998 that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the units had their respective commanders, but I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether there was any individual commander named Celiku other than Fatmir Limaj who was operating in that zone during May, June, July 1998.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, but I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There were other commanders named Celiku in addition to Fatmir Limaj. Is that correct, what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Celiku units had their own commanders, but I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that. I'll try to clarify my question and ask it in a better way. Did you know any individual KLA soldier who went by the nickname Celiku during May, June, July 1998 in the zone we've just been talking about, other than Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from Fatmir Limaj, I said I didn't know any commanders on that part of the road. It was only Fatmir I contacted with after I became acquainted with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I may have asked you this, but do you know who participated in forming the Celiku units? Which individual KLA soldiers or commanders were tasked with forming these units?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably someone from the General Staff, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Would the General Staff have dictated who was to form these units?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. Can you just explain what you meant by "probably somebody from the General Staff," your previous answer, "would have been responsible for forming these units," the Celiku units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it once again touches upon the problem and the danger that I touched upon a while back, in that the witness is being asked to speculate. This was a time of transition and flux, and he states he doesn't know and he's being asked to speculate. But really, it's not fair to the witness to ask him to go further than that. Your Honour, that's my observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. The question -- sorry, the answer of the witness which preceded the question indicated some regard for a role of the General Staff. The next question may clarify whether that was entirely speculative or based upon some knowledge, and we'll see. So if you would proceed, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I'll repeat the question. I won't go over it. You answered my question about who participated in the forming of the units with "probably somebody from the General Staff." And I asked you: "Would the General Staff have dictated who was to form these units?" And you said you didn't know. So I'm asking what you meant by "somebody from the General Staff" would have been involved in the formation of the Celiku units. Can you explain why you say that, that it would have been somebody in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said so, given my experience, why I am saying this. Because with commanders -- unit commanders I rallied around myself, there was present a member of the General Staff when they elected me as the commander of the Drenica operational zone. So present at that meeting was someone from the General Staff. That was why I said that if the other units merged and wanted to elect their commander, in this case Commander Celiku, I assumed that there must have been somebody from the General Staff. I may be wrong. Maybe there wasn't anyone. But just because of my experience I presume that they would have done the same. That was why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During May, June, July 1998 after your initial meeting with Fatmir Limaj, did you meet with him or speak with him again?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have often met him. I don't know what relevance this has. I have met him sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what would be the context of those meetings during that period?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- we met like friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where did you meet with your friend Fatmir Limaj during May, June, July 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I've lost track of when our next break is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is in this present area. If you're saying that's a convenient time for you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we're near, it would be fine and it may speed things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break now and resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General, thank you very much. I don't have anymore questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Again, the short straw I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: General, I represent Isak Musliu and I'd like to ask you some questions, if I may. The KLA was an entirely volunteer army, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning it was a voluntary army organised by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The answer you gave us just now begins with the words "in the beginning." Does that mean that there came a time when it became a conscription army, and do you understand what I mean by the question?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, everything was voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did that ever change?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the passing of time, the KLA developed and got restructured by forming brigades and the operational zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The KLA never had the power to force anyone to join it, did it?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: As far as those who joined are concerned, General - and I'm now concentrating on the early part of 1998 - some of the people who joined had had some military training in their lives. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Many had not. That is also right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: My next question deals with the period up to the formation of brigades, and it is this: As far as military discipline was concerned, would you agree, General, that it was at the very least very relaxed? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was not strict discipline, until the creation of the brigades. And it took some time to create them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And until the creation of the brigades, would it be fair to say as far as military discipline is concerned that as you told us yesterday there was often nothing anyone could do with a misbehaving soldier. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because everything was voluntary and they voluntarily -- could withdraw from the army if they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The death in March 1998 of Adem Jashari of itself brought forward many volunteers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: An expression from my country would be, General, that the death of Adem Jashari became a recruiting sergeant for the KLA. Do you understand what I mean by the question?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Drenica, that area, that geographic area of Kosovo was very much the place to which early volunteers used to go first. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And it was from Drenica, that geographic area, that these volunteers were spread out around Kosovo, I'm speaking now of the early months before the formation of brigades. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Part of them who came to join came to Drenica. I don't know whether all of them came to Drenica. Many of them did not come to Drenica, they went to their own areas. This -- it doesn't -- it is not -- it does not go without saying that everybody who came came to Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't think my question suggested the totality, but a large number came there first and I think you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't mean to interrupt. General, I want to try and summarise how the KLA developed during the spring and summer of 1998. And I wonder if you might consider this as a way of summarising the situation: Men joined; men joined other men and became units; units fought alongside each other; groups of units became zones; and eventually zones became brigades. Now, I hope I've taken that slowly. General, I'll repeat it if you like, but do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree with me? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: As far as the early stages are concerned - and now I've defined that I think twice already by being the period up to through the spring/summer of 1998 - it's right to say, is it not, General, that different zones developed their organisational abilities at different rates; some did it quicker than others. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And can we just look, please, together at these areas that became operational zones. And I want to do it through a map you were shown briefly yesterday. It's P1. Mr. Nicholls was showing it to you yesterday. It's map number 10, please, the last one. General, I hope this may be the shortest and most efficient way of doing this. First of all, would you look at this with me and would you please bear in mind that this was created by the British Ministry of Defence. All right. This is not created by anyone from the KLA. It says in the right-hand corner of it, if I read it properly: "Produced by Military Survey, Ministry of Defence, United Kingdom, 1998." But, General, it may be the case that you can agree with me that the British Ministry of Defence may have got something almost right. So let's have a look at it together, shall we. You see Lapusnik in the middle of the map there, above the S of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Above it, bounded by the red markings, is the described as Drenica. Does that correspond with your understanding of the zone that was to become the Drenica zone?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the area that we see here -- it could do with some improvement because there are many villages that are missing in this map, with regard to the Drenica operational area. I don't know how detailed this map is and the lines of responsibility, how detailed they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: General, because it was made by who it was made by, and no doubt based on information, and because of when it appears to be created of course I'm sure we all understand that it is not precisely accurate. And that's why I use the phrase "correspond to your general understanding of the layout." I just want to get the picture clear in the Court's mind and, indeed, in mine. Below Drenica and to the left of it as we look at the map, that is another operation or zone or area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Dukagjini area on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And as we walk around the map together, General, the next big area includes places like Suva Reka, which we know about; Orahovac, which we know about; is the Pastrik zone. Correct? You have to answer, General.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Of course approximately. Next to it now, as it were, the other side of a broken line, Nerodimlje; and next to that Karadak; and above that which includes Pristina itself, Shales. Now, again, approximately do you agree that is a reasonable representation of the way the operational zones came to be created?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I would say approximately because the boundaries of other zones -- I don't know them very well. I know the boundaries of my zone. But I think they are approximately accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were asked a lot of questions by Mr. Nicholls regarding units positioning themselves either side of the Pec-Peja road -- Pec-Pristina road. General, I want to be clear about it if we can. First of all, as far as you were concerned which units - and again in the spring and summer of 1998, which units were your responsibility? What were they called?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the spring after the 5th of March, it was only the Shkoza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It follows from that answer, does it not, General, that you had no personal responsibility with any Celiku unit, so-called? Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're very right when you say that because there was no such responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It follows from that answer also, does it not, General, that you had no responsibility -- personal responsibility for any Pellumbi or any other unit other than your own. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Until I was appointed commander, I did not have any responsibility on these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And so the Tribunal understands it, General, these units were separate units from each other; some had people in charge of them and some of them did not. Now, have I understood the position accurately or not?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every unit had a person who was in charge. I don't know about other units. And I did not know all of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Before I ask you some other questions of detail, I wonder whether I could ask your help to understand something that you had written on your behalf and which you signed, which was a letter addressed to this Tribunal. General, I don't know, do you have with you a copy of a letter written and dated the -- well, I don't know when it was written, but it's certainly dated the 24th of November, 2004, signed by you and your lawyer Mr. Krasniqi. Do you have that with you?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You don't. Well, General, it's important, perhaps, for the Tribunal to understand precisely what your position is in these proceedings, and I want your help then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can provide you a copy of that letter if you need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: General, you'll be given a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is this in English? Great. Your Honours have this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: My first question has to be this: Can you identify this as a letter that was signed by you in its original form and written on your behalf and in accordance with your instructions? Three questions in one, I'm afraid. First of all, was it written on your behalf? You have to answer, General.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was written on my behalf. I asked my lawyer to write down the reasons why, and he has written them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Was this letter written in accordance with your instructions to your lawyer, General? In other words, did you agree with its contents?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And is the original signed by you?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one has not been signed, but I agree that these are the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. things that I told him orally and he wrote them down and he submitted this to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: General, the important part of the letter was perhaps the second paragraph. And perhaps the most important part of that paragraph is what I shall read slowly to the end of it. "I will not be a witness for the Prosecution. But if the Defence proposes me, then I will be a witness for the Defence counsel of Fatmir Limaj. The reason is that, based on the political circumstances in Kosovo, my role as one of the first founders of KLA and later as Chief of Staff of the KLA and now as Deputy Commander of the KPC, this has had influence over my authority with the population." General, I'd like to understand and others may also join in that wish, to understand precisely what that sentence means. So as it was written on your behalf, would you be good enough to tell us what that means.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can say what is stated here and maybe elaborate it a little bit further, why that was written the way it was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If you would be so kind.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was this. I'll start from the beginning because I am under oath here. This is the second time I have taken an oath. The first time I took an oath under -- in front of my flag and my legendary commander; at the second time was here where I declared solemnly that I would say the truth and only the truth. I always was willing to come to the Tribunal and cooperate with the Tribunal because this is a democratic, independent Tribunal. And the first time I was sent a summons by Carla Del Ponte, I responded to that summons, before coming to today's point. Similarly, the office of the Defence asked me to be interviewed and I said that I would with pleasure give my interview to them. And I asked for the investigator from the OTP to be present. It is important to say that I have been at the disposal and still am at the disposal of the Tribunal, but with -- as regards my statement, this has one reason: because I have heard that in the Tribunal there will be other former commanders that have fought against the Serbian forces. And knowing that, knowing what kind of genocide the Serbian forces have committed on our people following the strategy of the Academy of Sciences led my Milosevic and applied by the Serbian commanders, starting from the general commander to the commander of a simple platoon, they inflicted such suffering upon my people. This was genocide, and we still don't know where many of the victims are, where their bodies lay. And to come and give testimony here in this Tribunal about my soldiers, the soldiers of the KLA who fought without uniforms, without guns, without weapons, I was not willing to come and testify here on behalf -- on the side of the OTP. That's the reason why. But however, the summons ordered me to come here to this Tribunal, and I accepted that because I was given the opportunity to speak the truth and only -- nothing but the truth, so say how things happened because we believe in justice. This was the reason. I can declare here in front of this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber, that I never hesitated to come and will never hesitate in the future so say the truth and to protect -- to defend the truth, to say the truth about the things that have happened to our people, the massacres that have happened in Kosova. Many of you and many of the public -- a great part of the public opinion don't still know what happened there, what really happened there. The next day I got the summons. The Prosecutor asked me whether I could meet the Defence and then I wanted them to be present because I wanted to be correct with both parties and I wanted to be transparent. And I have never met a Defence lawyer. I'm saying it again because I'm under oath, the oath that I took yesterday. There are many things that I said, many things that I might have forgotten, but what I have said are the truth. This is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: General, I want to read to you the last words virtually you spoke on tape to the Office of the Prosecutor when you were interviewed on the 19th of November, 2003. And I want to ask you at the end of what I shall read, which is only five or six lines, whether you stand by this now, today, or not. You said this - it's page 58 of the document if anyone wants to follow - "Every democratic country should come to terms with people who committed crimes during the war. Even countries that have perfected the system, the democratic system, still have problems, let alone us, who were just starting without any experience. There is no one above the law. People may do things in the euphoria of the moment, but afterwards they have to take responsibility." General, do you stand by those words today?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honourable Gentlemen, I've said it several times and I say it again: Nobody is above the law. I've said that. In many countries -- in any country things could happen, crimes of this sort. And I've said that because the state that exercised this genocide against us, it was an organised state, an organised army, an army with years of experience; while the KLA, we started to get organised in the conditions we were in, with what we could do in those circumstances. But in any country of the world, mistakes can be made. I'm not alluding here or pointing to a certain point or individual. But in whatever country this happens or might happen, these people should go and stand before the justice and pay for the crimes. But in Kosova, the only genocide that happened was carried out by the Serbian forces under Milosevic because they committed crimes against the whole civilian population of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: General, can I turn from, as it were, those general questions to some more specific ones. There was, by the autumn, August, September, October, of 1998, was there not, a plan or proposals that were being but into effect for the creation of brigades and operational zones? We've already established that, I think. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were to tell the Office of the Prosecutor in that same interview - again, if anyone wants to follow what I'm putting, it's page 16 - that "in 1998, the plan," these are your words, "starting being put in effect. I think they existed before that because I had no knowledge, no context, of what was going on in the General Staff. I don't know for sure, but more competent people will know." General, again, I think I should put it this way and I think you should be able to answer this question yes or no. Do you stand by that answer? Is that the position as far as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that because I was not a member of the General Staff of the -- and I couldn't have known what things were happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Right. Would you agree with me that Shukri Buja would be someone who would know what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say that. I don't know whether he knew or not. Probably not because he was not a member of the staff. If he were, he would have known, but as far as I know he wasn't a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Was he not promoted around June 1998 to be a commander within a subzone? Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if he became a member of the General Staff, I don't know when he became.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I have the advantage here. I'm looking at the statement he's made to this Tribunal, and so I have that in front of me. I want to put something to you for your comment, please. Were you aware of the creation or the discussion to create political zones in the early 1990s, in 1993 to be exact?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I was not a member of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The political plan at the time, it may be said, was based on the idea of liberating all Albanian territory. Were you aware of that being talked of in the early 1990s, General?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning of the 1990s when we started organising ourselves and joined the KLA, we did not fight for the whole territory of the Kosova. But I did not know about all these things that you mentioned now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I think in the light of that answer it might be fruitless for me to go on putting to you what Shukri Buja may eventually come and tell us himself, so I'll move on. I want to see if I can, with your assistance, paint a picture of the situation in the spring and summer of 1998 again, General. So we are talking about April, May, June, and so on, that period only for the moment. Was it still the case in that period that some men who were joining in the KLA had no weapon with which to fight? Was that still the position then?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were many cases when there were soldiers without weapons. That's true, yes. And very often it happened that the same weapon was used by one soldier and then used by another soldier when he had to rest because we did not have enough weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, let's contrast that position with a position later in the year, General, if we may. Doing the best you can and speaking only, please, from your experience. First of all, did that sort of situation change as 1998 wore on?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to weapons, we always lacked weapons, enough weapons. But we became consolidated later on and the situation improved. We still did not have enough weapons, but -- and also soldiers that did not have their own uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were issuing, were you not, General, documents that purported to be orders from where you were based. We saw one yesterday regarding people gathering together in public places. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I think in front of you will be some of these documents, and I just want to ask you about one or two of them if I may, please. Yes. Behind tab 3, first of all.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me that document, please, because I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I can't, but I know a man who will any minute now. General, I hope you're being given this in both English and Albanian.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: This seems to be dated the 27th of August, 1998, and it begins with the words: "On the basis of military law and the regulations of the Kosovo liberations and the need for the appointment of staff to the special unit of the operational subzone of Drenica I appoint," and you indicate appointment of someone there as a commander of a special unit. The second paragraph of this document I'm interested in, General. You appoint someone but you give him the right to appeal in the same document. Do you see that? If it's been translated properly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is written -- this has been written to the General Staff. They had to evaluate this person and then return -- come back with an answer for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And according to this document, if I've understood it correctly, General, if this person didn't like the decision presumably to appoint him, he could appeal against it. Is that what this document is saying?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had the opportunity to appeal it, yes. Or to propose something or to give his own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: To say, I don't want this job, how about giving it to somebody else. He could have said that, too, presumably.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the circumstances. If he had a very strong reason why not to take on that responsibility, we could have consultations and he could propose somebody else or give another idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: There was quite a lot of these discussions going on, wasn't there, with regard to the carrying out of orders and requests of commanders and so on within the KLA, wasn't there, General? If someone didn't like the idea of something, they could speak up, couldn't they? And were expected to. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could express their own opinion because we were re-organising. And when the units existed, all of us were equal. When the commanders were appointed, then we started to apply some of these rules, military rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can I turn to ask you some questions about Lapusnik itself, please.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The evidence you gave us a little earlier on today, if I've made an accurate note about it, when Mr. Nicholls, the gentleman over there, was asking you questions, you said that in May, June, and July you were not able to penetrate into Lapusnik itself.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sorry, General?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question once again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. You told us a little earlier on this afternoon that you were not able in May, June, and July of 1998 to, and I quote you I hope accurately, to penetrate into Lapusnik itself. Do you remember saying that to us a little earlier on today?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't get a translation.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the day -- it was the day when it was said about what was said in Lapusnik. When I went there, I was not able to penetrate into Lapusnik. It was not in May, June, or the months you mentioned. It was just a day during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I see. During the fighting, during the war, and before the end of July 1998, General, did you get yourself into the village of Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you taken to any buildings or houses or places in Lapusnik where there were other KLA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, think about it, please. Can you recollect now? Did you spend any period of time in Lapusnik, by which I mean did you ever stay overnight there during the war, the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've slept in many places, but I cannot remember the exact case, whether I stayed in Lapusnik. But it happened that I had to spend the night in many places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If I showed you -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If I showed you a photograph of a building or two, might that help you to remember or don't you think it would?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can show me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been better.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: General, you can't trust anyone these days, least of all lawyers. They take things from you when you least expect it, so sorry for the delay. General, could you be given P6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Hasan has it. He's come to the rescue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: General, just have a look at these photographs, if you would. Perhaps if you could have them all in front of you in one go to save time. Just have a look, please.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at the photographs. I see some building, some houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. This is the compound. Next one, please. No, that doesn't help you very much, it's an aerial shot. Can we get down on the ground, do you think? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's clearly seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Typical house, General, no doubt. But I'm asking -- this is a house in the village of Lapusnik. Do you remember -- recognise it at all?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Another building, same compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The one that looks like this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't recognise this either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The gates of the compound there, between a smaller building and the Oda.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is clearly -- it's clearly seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you recognise it as a place you may have visited or not?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to show you one other. I wonder if the usher there has a photograph that has a number 18 at the bottom. This is a different set of buildings now, across the road. Does that ring any bells with you, General?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not ring a bell with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The first series of photographs I showed you are said to be a prison camp run by soldiers of your army in the spring and summer of 1998 where people were held, tortured, and murdered. General, were you aware of the existence of such a place, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I have said this to the Prosecution because they have asked this many times and I said it was the first time that I heard of such a thing, when they brought Fatmir Limaj here. I've never heard of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I show you for the photos. General, I want to move on to another topic, please. And the reason I do so, it's military police, and the reason I do so is that my client became a member of the military police later on in 1998. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I should ask you I suppose this rather obvious question: Did you ever meet Isak Musliu, otherwise known as Qerqiz, as far as you recollect?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall I met him. It might be possible that I met him, but I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Now, General, I want to ask you, please, about the military police, and that is the reason why I do so. The first question: When to the best of your recollection were the military police of UCK formed?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, when the military police of the UCK was formed, I don't know. But in my zone, when the brigade started to get formed it was seen as reasonable and they started -- it was started to form also the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Therefore, if we are fixing it by when the brigades started to get formed, we must be talking, must we not, of a period after August, now into the autumn of 1998. Would you agree, General?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This goes until the fall of 1998 but also up to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were never able to consolidate it the way we wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, that's their creation. I want to look at their role with you, please. First of all, it's right, isn't it, that you in your area were responsible for the creation of the military police. So you had direct involvement in their creation in your area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my area, I started to assume the responsibility for the creation of the zone, and this started with the creation, formation, of the brigades as I mentioned earlier and with units or the military police in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The purpose, was it not I suggest, was to improve discipline within the ranks of the KLA. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besides discipline, they thought it reasonable to deal with caring the wounded, the policemen and civilians as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Page 44 of your interview with the OTP, at least page 44 of the English translation you say: "The main one," that is to say the duty, "was to discipline soldiers; that sometimes they had to keep law and order. That didn't happen very often. They were involved in fighting and looking after people who were wounded and so on." So general duties beyond that of discipline. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: They were given black uniforms to wear, were they not? Once they'd been created, of course. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: To, of course, distinguish them from other ranks and other units.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to go back, as it were, to the earlier days again, if I may, General, dealing with the position in May of 1998. What I want to suggest to you generally is this, and you would have had experience of this I suggest and certainly knowledge of it from your dealings with your comrades. In those early days when men were arriving across the border, they were very much making their own decisions about where they would go to take up the fight. Now, would you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No one would point them in any particular direction. Often they would simply get together and say, We've heard there's trouble in such-and-such a place. We better go and see what we can do. Of course I paraphrase it, General, of course I reduce it to its bare bones. But is that the position that existed in May of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately I can say yes because they were volunteers and they had no address, where to go, soldiers in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Indeed it wasn't until much later on in the summer, was it, that you even had a record of who had joined up. Would that be right? You didn't know the names even of all your comrades in your area. Would that be right, General?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not have the names of many of those who joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And as far as people going to places, I'll take -- pluck one out of thin air. Lapusnik, for example. Went to fight in Lapusnik. If they heard of a problem elsewhere, they would just up and go there, wouldn't they? Didn't need an order; didn't need a request. They'd just do it off their own backs, as we would say in England. Do you have experience of that happening, General?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from my experience. As long as we were operating like units, they acted voluntarily and went voluntarily there. Because if they knew another unit and it was -- that thing was happening there, and that's why that other unit came to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And that situation, I suggest, in reality lasted until such times as the brigades were formed. Now, would you agree with that, General, as a general proposition?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If Your Honours just give me a moment, I think I've finished. Yes, I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's all I ask you, General. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: General, I represent Fatmir Limaj. Hopefully we may be able to get through my questions for you this evening. You say that after the death of Adem Jashari there was a huge influx of people that swelled the ranks of the KLA. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And it was quite a challenge, it was quite difficult, for the KLA to assimilate and absorb these people. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And in fact, one of the major challenges of the KLA through the major part of 1998 in addition to surviving against the Serbs and fighting was to try to give some semblance of organisation to these civilians that were joining the ranks of the Kosovo Liberation Army. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Going back to the beginning of the conflict up to June 1998, you say that -- well, apart from the KLA, are you aware of other armed groups operating in Kosovo up until June 1998 against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of other groups apart from the KLA and the Serbian forces. If the paramilitary forces existed or various forces, I was not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Had you heard of a group called the National Movement for the Liberation of Kosova?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not heard of such a group at the time. If you're talking about the LKCK, yes I've heard about that. But I've not heard about the National Movement for the Liberation of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, the LKCK, that operated until what period of time? Are you familiar with that or not?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group had started its activity even earlier on. I don't know about its later activity, but you better ask those who've been responsible in the LKCK or the members of the General Staff who are in charge of that movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of an aware, and forgive my pronunciation, it's atrocious, the region of Belacevac?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the area -- the region of Belacevac. There were members of the KLA who fought there, but it was under the reign of the UKLA [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And what area or what zone was that area of Belacevac in, do you remember that? What zone of operations was that in?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belacevac is included in the border of the operational zone of Drenica and also the operational zone of Shales and its bordering the operational zone of Shales.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And do you remember what KLA units operated in that zone?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You say that after September 1998 that you became aware of Fatmir Limaj as a commander of the 121st Brigade. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was only then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And at that time you were also a brigade commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was a zone commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, a zone commander. Now, are you aware of displaced civilians being present in the Pastrik zone?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were displaced civilians in my zone as well, but also in the Pastrik zone as well. Displaced civilians were more placed in Pastrik zone other than other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And these were civilians, largely, that had fled the onslaught from the Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. They found it a safer place, a shelter, and they went there from various places, went to that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. And indeed these were civilians, often, who fled their homes in extreme fear with very little other than what was on their back. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And the condition that these civilians lived in was extremely difficult. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: There was a huge shortage of food, medicines, clothes, children's nappies, diapers, the rest of it. Things were very difficult for these civilians, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they lacked the elementary means. They did not even have bread to eat, let alone clothes and other things, which -- there was a huge shortage of those things and they were in a miserable state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Can you describe -- let me ask you one question and hopefully we can finish for the day. Are you aware of how Fatmir Limaj dealt with these civilians in his area? And if so, could you describe that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have liked to be in the position of Fatmir Limaj to render help to those people who suffered, and I would have done the same thing and rendered help to those people and population who were around that area. However, with all the difficulties and the circumstances in that area, Fatmir and -- with his soldiers and his friends and his group, rendered help to those people. And this is such a thing -- this has to be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we can leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Well, that clearly is a time when we must break for the day. General, the time has come when we must finish once again. I would ask that you return tomorrow. I think we can be confident that you will complete your evidence tomorrow afternoon. We will start at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that Mr. Cayley is in court and I know that he's come to bid his farewell. May I please simply be permitted to say on behalf of the Defence bar in this case that it's been a great pleasure to have Mr. Cayley as an opponent. If I may be permitted to say he has acted throughout in the very finest traditions of the English bar. We will be sorry to see him go. We'll be sorry to lose him, but he wish him well in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. You indeed had perceived Mr. Cayley. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will be very brief. And to make it clear for the purposes of the record, you know that I've already written to the Chamber a letter which was copied to the Defence explaining that I was leaving the Tribunal. There's nothing unusual in this, Your Honours, there's no connection with this case. This was a move that was planned over a year ago and which I knew and indeed the Prosecutor knew was going to take place. The case will be supervised from now on by Mr. Alex Whiting. There will be another trial attorney that's joining the team towards the end of this month, Milbert Shin. I'd only like to thank you, the Chamber, for your patience over the time that I've been leading the case and your attention. And I'd also, obviously, like to thank Mr. Topolski for his very kind comments about me. So with that, Your Honours, I bid you farewell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, we share the views expressed so generously by Mr. Topolski. We have been much assisted by the work you've put into this case. We wish you well in your new position, and we look forward to the continued assistance we'll receive from the other members of the team that you leave behind. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of January, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
